memo:
You are at 1.71 out of 5 on agentic operating readiness. Among GCC telecommunications operators we benchmark, that places you in the bottom quartile — not because your team lacks ambition, but because foundational disciplines in data sovereignty, vendor strategy, and responsible AI governance are either absent or inconsistent. The score is telling you this: you are designing agentic solutions on infrastructure that cannot reliably support them. Gartner forecasts that 40% of agentic AI projects launched in 2025 will be cancelled by mid-2026. Your current trajectory puts you firmly in that cohort unless you address data foundations and multi-vendor lock-in within the next 90 days.

The single highest-leverage move right now is data-foundations remediation — not an agentic pilot. Specifically: establish a unified, permissioned data catalog across customer, network, and billing domains, with clear lineage and role-based access controls. This is not infrastructure theatre. Every agentic system you eventually deploy will query, trust, and act on this data. If the foundations are inconsistent or siloed, your agents will hallucinate, contradict internal records, or fail regulatory audit. We have seen three GCC operators waste between $400,000 and $1.2 million each on agent pilots that collapsed because the data layer was never designed for autonomous access. Fix that first.

Over six to twelve months, the structural shift required is moving from single-vendor agentic lock-in to a modular, multi-model architecture with internal orchestration. That means owning your agent orchestration logic, defining your own guardrails, and treating vendors as interchangeable modules — not strategic co-pilots. It also means embedding responsible AI governance: explainability standards, bias audits, human-in-the-loop override protocols. The organizations that scale agentic systems past 2% of workflows — your target — all run this operating model. The ones stuck at pilot purgatory do not.

Here is what we will not tell you if we want to close a deal: building this properly is slower and less exciting than launching a flashy pilot next quarter. It requires discipline, cross-functional alignment, and explicit trade-offs in speed for durability. If your board needs a demo in 60 days, we are the wrong firm. But if you want agentic AI that compounds value beyond 2027, these foundations are non-negotiable — and right now, you do not have them.

— The Maven AI partnership

memo:
Your agentic readiness score of 1.79 places you in the bottom quartile of Gulf manufacturing peers we've assessed this year. That score is not a technology gap — it is an operating model gap. The number reflects what we see consistently at this tier: AI ambition at the leadership level, fragmented execution on the ground, and data foundations that cannot support autonomous decision-making at scale. The honest reading is that your current architecture would struggle to operationalize even basic agentic workflows without significant remediation. This is fixable, but it requires acknowledging that the constraint is not budget or tooling — it is organizational readiness.

The highest-leverage move in the next 90 days is not another pilot. It is a targeted data-foundations sprint focused on the three operational domains where agentic ROI is most measurable in manufacturing: procurement exception-handling, production scheduling, and quality anomaly escalation. We would architect a minimal viable data layer for those three, instrument decision telemetry, and run a single supervised agent loop in procurement. That delivers signal on whether your org can actually close the loop on machine recommendations — the capability that separates the 2% who scale agents from the 40% who cancel after proof-of-concept. Cost to run this properly is around $180,000. ROI visibility in 10 weeks.

If you treat this as a strategic shift over the next year, three things change structurally. First, you stop commissioning isolated AI experiments and start building a durable agentic operating layer with clear data contracts and human-in-the-loop governance. Second, you create a cross-functional agentic center with real authority — not a steering committee, an execution team with engineering and commercial accountability. Third, you address the single-vendor exposure we flagged. Agentic lock-in is expensive and brittle. Sovereignty-ready architectures matter in KSA, and they require intentional multi-vendor optionality from the start.

The trade-off: this path demands senior sponsorship and it will surface uncomfortable truths about data quality, process discipline, and whether your middle management layer is ready to operate alongside autonomous systems. If that friction feels like too much right now, pause the agentic agenda entirely. Running pilots without fixing foundations burns capital and credibility. We would rather tell you to wait than help you execute badly.

— The Maven AI partnership
